claims.text: Controlled-heating molecular dynamics simulations can capture the size-dependent thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have lower melting or transformation temperatures than larger particles or bulk material.
The reduced thermal stability of smaller nanoparticles is caused by amplified surface-energy effects.
The modeled nanoparticles have uniform chemical composition.
The modeled nanoparticles initially have relaxed crystalline structures.
A simulated heating ramp can induce melting or other structural phase changes in the nanoparticles.
Comparing different nanoparticle sizes under identical heating rates and simulation conditions isolates the size dependence of thermal response.
The interatomic potential must be validated for a multicomponent FeCuCrCoNi-type HEA system.
Smaller nanoparticles have a greater surface-to-volume ratio.
A greater surface-to-volume ratio enhances surface-atom mobility.
A greater surface-to-volume ratio alters local bonding environments relative to bulk material.
Enhanced surface-atom mobility promotes an earlier onset of melting or structural disordering.
During heating, surface premelting nucleates and propagates inward through the nanoparticle.
The critical melting or phase-change temperature decreases systematically as nanoparticle size is reduced.
The reduction in thermal stability of small nanoparticles is a significant fraction of the bulk value.
Bulk FeCuCrCoNi or sufficiently large nanoparticles exhibit higher thermal stability than smaller nanoparticles.
The predicted behavior is limited to idealized simulation conditions for FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Potential-dependent interactions and limited access to long-time diffusion events create uncertainty in the simulation results.
The magnitude of thermal-stability reduction depends on the interatomic-potential parameters, heating rate, and simulation timescale.
Abrupt changes in potential energy and radial distribution function can be used to identify the critical melting or transformation temperature.
